questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $det(A)=12.$ The matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ and ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+2{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(B)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+2{R}_{3}$ involves adding a multiple of one row to another row,  so it does not change the determinant.

Therefore, we only have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-det(A) \\  & =-(12) \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $det(A)=det(B),$ which of the following elementary row operations transforms matrix $A$ to matrix $B,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 5 & -4 & -3 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 5 & -4 & -3 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}| & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 6 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1}.
$$

questions.problem: Suppose $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $det(A)=-4.$ What is the value of $det(6A)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A)={k}^{n}\cdot det(A).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=6$ and $n=2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(6A) & ={6}^{2}\cdot det(A) \\  & =36\cdot (-4) \\  & =-144.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose $Y$ is a $6\times 6$ matrix and $det(Y)=5.$ What is the value of $det(2Y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Multiplying a $n\times n$ matrix by a scalar $k$ is equivalent to multiplying each row by $k,$ and this occurs $n$ times. This leads to the result

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot Y)={k}^{n}\cdot det(Y).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have $k=2$ and $n=6.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(2Y) & ={2}^{6}\cdot det(Y) \\  & =64\cdot 5 \\  & =320.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Suppose $B$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $det(B)=-7.$ The matrix $C$ is obtained from $B$ by applying the elementary row operations ${R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}$ and ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}.$ What is the value of $det(C)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's figure out what each operation does to the determinant.

- The operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}$ involves swapping two rows, so it changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.

- The operation ${R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}$ involves multiplying a row by $2,$ so the determinant is multiplied by $2$ as well.

Therefore, we have to change the sign of the determinant to the opposite one and multiply by $2$ as well. Consequently, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(C) & =2\cdot (-det(B)) \\  & =-2det(B) \\  & =-2\cdot (-7) \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$
